notes.AS04: The passage shows grief as something that can run deep and long: Jacob mourns for many days and will not be comforted. It speaks to the weight of mourning a parent. It is a father's grief for a son he loved, so it says nothing about guilt or about a parent who was unkind.
notes.AS06: This is a child's account of parting from her mother, and what it records is regret, not relief. It touches your situation only in one place: the writer says she no longer felt free to voice her own feelings. The passage does not speak to relief after caring for a parent.
notes.AS07: The passage turns to how one speaks with someone in grief. It says to meet them in conversation, even to groan along with them, but not to groan inwardly as well. It does not say how often to check in or when to leave someone alone, so it speaks only to the worry about what to say.
notes.AS12: Thoreau writes that people are often lonelier among others than when alone, and that solitude is not measured in miles between people. That echoes the loneliness you describe while sitting beside someone. The passage comes from a writer who loves being alone, and it does not say what companionship is supposed to feel like.
notes.AS14: The passage describes letting go of resentment by thinking, they did wrong to me, but what can I possibly do. It speaks to the part of your situation where you were treated badly. It says nothing about checking his accounts, blocking him, or the part of you that is still waiting.
notes.AS16: The passage says everything has two handles, and that when a brother acts unjustly one may hold the matter by the fact that he is a brother, raised alongside. It speaks only to the sibling side of what you describe. It says nothing about your parents blaming you or shouting when you raise it.
notes.AS20: This passage is written to sisters in a religious community about love of neighbour. It counsels giving way to others' wishes and putting their interests ahead of one's own, even at some cost. It speaks to the strain between you and your family. It does not say whether to move or how to keep the relationships intact.
notes.AS21: Gibran lists the clothes, meals and beds that come from other people's hands, and asks how anyone can separate from others. That speaks to the sense of owing your family a great deal. It is a statement about how bound people are to each other. It does not address becoming independent or guilt.
notes.AS28: The passage is the voice of someone cut off from friends, shut in, and calling out daily. That speaks to what your girlfriend is going through when she is left out again. It comes from the one who is excluded, so it does not say what to say to her or how to help.
notes.AS30: The passage is about the speaker's own words, including sharp words said to someone's face. It says that if they are untrue or pointless they should not be spoken, and that even true ones need the right time. That bears on how your manager speaks to you. It does not address pushing through or leaving, or your racing heart.
notes.AS34: Seneca says that someone who keeps looking back to count what they can carry out will never get out, because no one swims ashore with their luggage. That speaks to your fear of having no job and to the pull of what the income provides. The passage does not say how to leave or how people manage it.
notes.AS39: The passage says money wrings tears and toil from people, and that owning wealth brings its own worry. It speaks to the tears over money you describe. Its subject is greed and the anxieties of those who hold riches, not debt that grows despite careful living, so it fits only part of what you wrote.
notes.AS45: The passage says to be not afraid, not to count how many times one has failed, and to go forward, for time is endless. It speaks to the fear and to facing something a second time. It is about repeated effort, not illness, so it says nothing about the diagnosis itself.
notes.AS57: The writer of this passage speaks of an impulse to end his life, held back by the thought of his father, and of commanding himself to live. He says living can itself be an act of bravery. It speaks only to staying alive. It says nothing about wrongdoing or about forgiving oneself.
notes.AS58: The passage is the cry of someone betrayed by a close friend, one they trusted and shared meals with. It speaks to the trust that was broken. It places the act with the friend who turned on them, and it says nothing about wondering whether one encouraged it.
notes.AS61: The passage tells of Abram being told to leave his country, relatives and father's house for a land God would show him. It speaks to leaving home and family behind. It says nothing about whether such a move is right in the long run, or about work or children.
notes.AS63: The passage says that to improve, one should be content to be thought foolish about externals, and that even those who seem to be somebody should distrust themselves. It speaks to the gap you describe between how others see you and how you see yourself. It does not address feeling like a child in an adult's role.
notes.AS66: The passage gives voice to a heart asking why God does not speak or come. It says such thoughts arrive in low moments and then are forgotten. That speaks to the long silence you describe. It does not say what a person might be doing wrong, and it does not mention Mass or daily prayer.
notes.AS69: Marcus Aurelius writes that principles die only if the thoughts behind them go out, and that recovering one's life lies in looking at things again as one used to. That speaks to your goals feeling meaningless afterwards. It is his counsel for regaining a settled mind, and it says nothing about an accident or a brush with death.
notes.AS76: The passage describes someone who lies down to sleep unafraid, full of sympathy for all living creatures. That matches, in spirit, the sleeping dog resting his head on your knee. The passage is about the Buddha's own peace and kindness, so it speaks only to the sleep and the tenderness toward a living creature.
notes.H03: The passage says days are past, plans are broken off, and so are the thoughts of the heart. That speaks to the sudden end of the relationship and the fear you describe about the future you now face. It says nothing about the anger or about whose fault it was.
notes.H06: The passage says young people lose heart at a first failure, yet someone who keeps trying 'has not one chance, but a hundred chances.' That speaks to the weight you put on this one rejection after working so long toward it. It doesn't speak to the sadness itself, only to the idea that a single outcome is not all there is.
notes.H07: The passage describes grief at the loss of a dear friend: everything darkened, every place hated for lacking him, eyes searching everywhere. That speaks to losing your dog, whom you call your closest friend and your reason to come home each day. The passage names the grief rather than offering a way through it.
notes.H08: The passage says some of our children are our justifications and some are our regrets. It touches the fear you describe of holding a grudge, or of feeling like a bad parent, depending on which way you choose. It doesn't say anything about how to weigh career against time with your children.
notes.H10: The passage says everything has two handles, one by which it can be borne and one by which it cannot. About a brother who acts unjustly, it suggests holding the matter by the fact that he is family, not by the injustice. That speaks to the fighting with your mother. It doesn't speak to the guilt you feel or to whether there is a way out.
notes.H12: The passage says that when you isolate yourself everything hurts, and that feeling for others brings help. That speaks to the loneliness you describe and the sense of being alone with your own thoughts. It doesn't speak to the times you approached people and it went badly.
notes.H14: The passage is about keeping faith with a friend, and says that revealing his secrets destroys the friendship. That speaks to one side of your dilemma, the worry about betraying your friend. It says nothing about the wife or what might be owed to her, so it covers only half of what you describe.
notes.H15: The passage says that doing lower work does not make a lower person, and that people should be judged by the manner and spirit in which they do their duties. That speaks to the belittling you describe from your boss. It doesn't address the credit taken for your work, being held at your level, or the job market.
notes.H16: The passage speaks of ceasing to desire what one has long desired, and of living each day as a complete life, regarding it as possibly the last. That speaks to your unease at turning 58 and at how much you may not have achieved. It doesn't speak to where the years went.
notes.H18: The passage says this world is a means to an end, not an end in itself, and that we take life as the goal because we forget that we die. That speaks to your question about the point of it all when everyone dies. Its answer comes from its own faith: a purpose beyond this life.
notes.H19: The passage asks whether crying out that a room is dark will make the darkness go, and says that bringing in light makes it vanish. That speaks to the war, cruelty and ugliness you see everywhere you turn. It doesn't speak to how the darkness creeps into you, only to light as the answer to darkness.
notes.H20: The passage says the question is not whether we wear a religious habit but whether we submit our will to God's. It comes from a devout faith, so it touches your situation only loosely, at the point of outward act versus inner belief. It says nothing about conversion, about honesty in doing something you don't believe in, or about being accepted as you are.
notes.H21: The passage says a close friend, someone trusted who shared bread, has turned against the speaker. That speaks to your best friend telling your boyfriend after you confided in her. It doesn't say why such a betrayal happens, so it doesn't answer your question about why she did it.
notes.H22: The passage says that leaving church at every false sentiment would mean never staying five minutes, and it asks 'why come out?' since the street, the house and one's own speech are just as false. That speaks to the behaviour you describe at church. It doesn't speak to the sense that it has all become meaningless for you.
notes.H24: The passage says that guarding and beautifying the mind protects and renews the body, and that a sour face is made by sour thoughts. It speaks to your dread of the mirror only by turning attention from the body to the mind. It says nothing about comparing yourself with others, and its claims are the author's own.
notes.H25: The passage says that what one person dreads losing, another would not notice, and asks why anyone should judge others by their own standard. It fits your situation only loosely, through the idea that a measure which weighs heavily on one person is not shared by all. It doesn't speak to the comment that hurt you, your eating, or your long effort to lose weight.
notes.H28: The passage says that when a parent puts himself in the child's place and sees with him, that shared perception guides them both, but ordering from outside by guessing means the child will never obey. That speaks to the harshness you describe and the distance now. It doesn't speak to the guilt or to how to mend things.
notes.H29: The passage says that if another is preferred over you, you ought to rejoice for him if the things are good. It is about being the one passed over, which is the position you suspect your wife is in. It says nothing about why she responded as she did or what she feels.
notes.H30: The passage says 'my father gives me nothing' is all that happened, and that calling it an evil is added from outside, so what must be removed is the opinion about poverty, not the poverty. That speaks to the anger tied to your childhood. It doesn't speak to the hurt you describe, or to why money hasn't eased it.
notes.H32: The passage describes a smile, talk of nothing, and a feeling that this was what the speaker had long been waiting for. That echoes your engagement after years of hoping to find someone. It speaks to the waiting and its end, and says nothing more about the day itself.
